articles.author: Michael Amachree
articles.description:
It’s Day 4 of 12 Days of Svelte Apps 🎄
When things get hectic, Markdown keeps your plans:
structured
readable
easy to reuse
easy to share (or keep private)
Today’s mini-app is a clean Markdown Editor powered by Carta-MD, with a preview that updates as you type.
🔗 Try it live: https://svelte-apps.me/apps/markdown-editor
💻 View the code: https://github.com/Michael-Obele/Svelte-MiniApps/tree/main/src/routes/apps/(app)/markdown-editor
You don’t need a complicated system — you need:
headings to chunk your life into sections
checkboxes for “done / not done”
links for tickets, receipts, wishlists, and recipes
Bonus: the editor auto-saves your content to localStorage, so you can close the tab and come back later without losing your work.
Paste this into the editor and customize it:
   # Holiday Plan 🎄

   ## Gifts
   - [ ] Finalize gift list
   - [ ] Order online gifts
   - [ ] Wrap gifts
   - [ ] Label + stash

   ## Dinner
   - [ ] Decide menu
   - [ ] Buy groceries
   - [ ] Prep dessert
   - [ ] Set cooking timeline

   ## Travel
   - [ ] Confirm bookings
   - [ ] Pack chargers
   - [ ] Print tickets / download passes

Use - [ ] for tasks and - [x] for completed items.
Add links inline: [Recipe](https://example.com).
Keep one “Notes” section at the bottom for last-minute ideas.
That’s it. Simple structure beats complicated systems.
articles.title: Day 4: Plan the Holidays in Markdown (Markdown Editor) 📝

articles.author: Michael Amachree
articles.description:
It’s Day 3 of 12 Days of Svelte Apps 🎄
Holiday season is basically a memory test:
gift ideas
card messages
recipes and substitutions
travel details
“what was that link again?”
Today’s featured mini-app solves that in the cleanest way possible: Note Taker — a simple, fast place to capture notes without burying them in a pile.
🔗 Try it live: https://svelte-apps.me/apps/note-taker
💻 View the code: https://github.com/Michael-Obele/Svelte-MiniApps/tree/main/src/routes/apps/(app)/note-taker
If you only do one thing, do this:
Create a note per person and treat it like a tiny “gift profile”:
Gift Ideas — Mom
Gift Ideas — Dad
Gift Ideas — Partner
Then paste everything inside it:
sizes, colors, preferences
product links
reminders like “already owns this”
Write card drafts when inspiration hits (not when you’re standing over a blank card with a pen).
save a few variants
tweak later
copy/paste when you’re ready
Use one note as a cooking scratchpad:
timings you adjusted
substitutions that worked
“next time: double the sauce”
Once you’ve written a bunch of notes, finding them quickly is everything. The app includes a search box that filters notes by title or content, so “scarf” or “cinnamon” gets you to the right place fast.
If you’re logged in, you’ll see a manual sync button. The app also schedules sync attempts intelligently (only when you’re online and the tab is visible), so it doesn’t spam requests in the background.
Paste these into your first notes:
Gift Ideas — Alex
Idea: wool scarf (green)
Size: one-size
Link: …
Backup: candle set
Holiday Inbox
“Grandma likes peppermint bark”
“Find wrapping paper that matches”
“Remember: batteries”
Simple structure beats complicated systems — especially in December.
Tomorrow we’ll go deeper into planning workflows with a Markdown Editor.
articles.title: Day 3: Holiday Notes That Don’t Get Lost (Note Taker) 🗒️

articles.author: Deepak Mishra
articles.description:
1. Introduction


In modern web application development, the synchronous request-response cycle is often a bottleneck. Operations such as generating complex PDF reports, processing video uploads, or training machine learning models can take minutes or even hours. Blocking a standard HTTP request for this duration is unacceptable; it degrades user experience and ties up server resources, often leading to timeouts from reverse proxies like Nginx.
The standard solution is to offload these heavy operations to a distributed task queue like Celery. This decouples the execution from the web server. However, this decoupling introduces a new challenge: observability. Once a task is sent to the background, the web server loses track of it. How do we tell the user that their report is 50% complete?
T…

log.info('Connected')
log.error('Something broke')

Output:

💡 INFO    Connected
🔴 ERROR   Something broke

Just a bit of color and structure — but it makes a difference when you're debugging.
